solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Coat to take to the cleaners (6)

blocks.note: a sheep's woolly coat, or a warm zip-up jacket
slang for swindling someone out of all their money

annotation.surface: Someone dropping a coat off at the dry cleaner's.
annotation.walkthrough: "Take to the cleaners" is slang for cheating someone of their money, not a laundry errand, and that is the second meaning of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain: the woolly coat of a sheep, and the verb for stripping a victim of cash as a sheep is stripped of wool.

entries.clue: First of foot sloggers ordered Gallic dish (5,4)

indicatorNotes.First of: the first of a word is its opening letter
indicatorNotes.ordered: letters that are ordered are put into a new order

blocks.note: first letter of FOOT
SLOGGERS rearranged

annotation.surface: Foot soldiers who slog along being ordered a French meal.
annotation.walkthrough: "Foot sloggers" reads as one phrase for infantry, but only the first letter of "foot" is used and "sloggers" is the anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: frogs' legs are the dish most associated with French cooking, and Gallic means French.

entries.clue: Something to heat water, eg (7)

blocks.note: the heating coil in a kettle or immersion heater
water was one of the four classical building blocks of matter, with earth, air and fire

annotation.surface: An instruction to put water on to boil.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about boiling water, but it splits after "heat": water is itself an example of an element in the ancient sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the heating part inside a kettle, and one of the ancient four elements, of which water is an example.

entries.clue: Stroke edge (5)

blocks.note: a swimming stroke, the fast front one most swimmers learn
to edge forward is to move very slowly

annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns (a stroke, an edge), but "edge" is a verb here: to edge along a ledge is to crawl.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: front crawl is a swimming stroke, and to crawl is to edge slowly forward.

entries.clue: Oval racer to have in mind, mostly (5,3)

indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a shop that has goods in stocks them
CARE (mind, as in "mind the baby") without its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone keeping a racing car in their thoughts.
annotation.walkthrough: "Have in mind" looks like one phrase, but it splits after "in": to have in is to stock, and "mind" is CARE.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: stock car racing is run on oval tracks, so the car is an oval racer.

entries.clue: Royals meet Irish jockeys, keeping a kid around (5,9)

indicatorNotes.jockeys: to jockey is to jostle for position, so the letters are pushed around
indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so the shuffled letters hold the rest inside them

blocks.note: MEET IRISH rearranged, to be split THEIRM…IES
A + JEST; to kid around is to jest

annotation.surface: The royal family meeting Irish jockeys, with a child in tow.
annotation.walkthrough: Ireland and racing go together, so "Irish jockeys" reads as riders; "jockeys" is the verb telling MEET IRISH to shift around A JEST.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal title used as a plural noun: Their Majesties is how a king and queen together are referred to.

entries.clue: I supposedly run in fear (4,5)

blocks.note: reads as a coward confessing to fleeing; really the speaker is a liquid that runs down the skin
the circumstance: the kind brought on by fright is said to be chilly

annotation.surface: A coward confessing to running away when scared.
annotation.walkthrough: The "I" seems to be a person fleeing, but it is the sweat talking: sweat runs, and in a fright it is said to run cold.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a cold sweat is the clammy perspiration that breaks out when you are afraid, and sweat runs.

entries.clue: Note this, oddly, when stuffing chicken (7)

indicatorNotes.oddly: oddly means taking the odd-numbered letters, the 1st and 3rd of "this"
indicatorNotes.stuffing: stuffing a bird means filling its inside, so these letters go inside the chicken

blocks.note: a capon is a fattened cockerel
1st and 3rd letters of THIS

annotation.surface: A note about stuffing a chicken, like a line in a recipe.
annotation.walkthrough: "Stuffing chicken" reads as kitchen talk, and the bird really is stuffed here, only with letters instead of sage and onion.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in one sense: a caption is a short note printed beneath a picture.

entries.clue: Farm managed to get support from church (5)

indicatorNotes.to get support from: in a down answer the upper part is supported by what sits below it

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

annotation.surface: A struggling farm kept going with help from the local church.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down answer the lower part holds up the upper one, so the church sits underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a ranch is a large farm, especially an American cattle farm.

entries.clue: CBI — highest few, I fancy? (3,5,6)

indicatorNotes.fancy: to fancy is to imagine, and imagined letters are reworked into a new form

blocks.note: CBI + HIGHEST FEW + I rearranged

annotation.surface: A cynical remark that the business lobby is run by a small elite.
annotation.walkthrough: The CBI is the Confederation of British Industry, the UK's main bosses' lobby. The whole clue is both the fodder and a description of its leaders; the question mark flags the jokey definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue guesses that the CBI's highest few are its bosses, and big white chiefs is jocular slang for bosses.

entries.clue: On hand (9)

blocks.note: a law or machine that is on is in force, working
a factory hand, a worker

annotation.walkthrough: "On hand" reads as one phrase meaning available, but the two words are separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an adjective meaning in force or working, and a noun for a worker, as a hand is.

entries.clue: One in bed, some still up indeed (5)

indicatorNotes.some: some of the words means only part of them, so the answer is a run of letters inside

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of STILL through UP into the start of INDEED

annotation.surface: Someone in bed, and some still up: a household at night.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bed" suggests sleep, but it is a flower bed, and the thing in it is a plant.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the lupin is a tall garden flower grown in beds.

entries.clue: Go for hiding wife’s bulge (5)

indicatorNotes.hiding: to hide something is to keep it inside, out of view, so one part goes within the other

blocks.note: an item that goes for £5 sells for £5
W = wife, as in genealogies

annotation.surface: A husband urged to go and conceal his wife's bump.
annotation.walkthrough: "Go for" sounds like an attack; it means fetch a price, as in "it went for a song".
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a swell is a bulge or rounded rise, as in the swell of a hill.

entries.clue: Gold medal held by dating writer (9)

indicatorNotes.held by: something held by another is inside its grip, so the gold and medal go inside

blocks.note: a person dating someone is "with" them
OR is gold in heraldry
DSM is the Distinguished Service Medal

annotation.surface: An award-winning author with a medal, who is seeing someone.
annotation.walkthrough: "Gold medal" reads as one Olympic prize, but it splits into two parts; "dating" is about going out with someone, not a date on a calendar.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a wordsmith is a skilled writer.

entries.clue: Be as killers are, next time out (11)

indicatorNotes.out: out can mean disordered, as a joint put out, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ARE NEXT TIME rearranged

annotation.surface: A promise that the killers will be out, next time round.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition stops at "killers": to exterminate is to act as killers do. "Are" belongs to the fodder, though it seems to finish the phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: to exterminate is to kill off wholesale, which is what killers do.

entries.clue: Carpet salesman on edge, too (9)

blocks.note: a sales rep, short for representative
a rim is an edge
and = also, too

annotation.surface: A carpet salesman who is nervous as well.
annotation.walkthrough: "Carpet salesman" is one person in the surface, but "carpet" is a verb: to carpet someone is to haul them in for a telling-off.
annotation.definitionFit: A British idiom: to carpet an employee is to reprimand them, from being called onto the boss's carpet.

entries.clue: Anything but new books (3)

blocks.note: N = new
OT = Old Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: A reader wanting any books except new ones.
annotation.walkthrough: "Anything but new" reads as secondhand; the definition is only "Anything but", as in "anything but happy".
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: "anything but" negates what follows, as in "it was anything but easy".

entries.clue: Hermit’s last to start getting stick over month in France (9)

indicatorNotes.last to start: the last letter is sent to the start, the front of the word
indicatorNotes.over: over means turned over, and in a down answer that reads the stick upside down

blocks.note: HERMIT with its final T moved to the front
a rod is a stick, then turned over to DOR

annotation.surface: A hermit finally starting to pick up a walking stick during a month in France.
annotation.walkthrough: Thermidor, the heat month, was the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar, which is why it is a month "in France".
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: Thermidor was a month (mid-July to mid-August) in the calendar of Revolutionary France.

entries.clue: Total a few declared (3)

indicatorNotes.declared: declared means spoken out, so the answer is a word that sounds like the wordplay

blocks.note: some = a few; the spoken word is spelt differently here

annotation.surface: An accountant announcing a small total.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words are pronounced alike, so saying "a few" gives the word for a total.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sum is the total you get by adding up.

entries.clue: First man grabs drunk, upset waltzing girl (7)

indicatorNotes.grabs: to grab is to take hold of, so the first man takes the drunk inside
indicatorNotes.upset: to upset something is to tip it over, and in a down answer that turns it upside down

blocks.note: Adam, the first man in Genesis
lit = drunk, slang

annotation.surface: A drunk grabbed by a man, upsetting a girl who is dancing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Waltzing" is not a dance step here: "Waltzing Matilda" is the Australian folk song, and the girl is the one in its title.
annotation.definitionFit: An allusion: Matilda is the name in the song "Waltzing Matilda".

entries.clue: Unnecessary spin? Still, submit (11)

blocks.note: PR = public relations, the business of spin
still = even, as in "still/even better"
to table a motion is to submit it

annotation.surface: Someone who thinks the spin is pointless but gives in anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: "Submit" looks like giving in; it means put forward, as a motion is tabled in a British meeting.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: something preventable, such as an accident, did not need to happen.

entries.clue: Is grazing ridges around Kent area (7)

indicatorNotes.around: around means surrounding, so the ridges go either side of the area

blocks.note: the brow of a hill is its ridge
Kent is a county in South-East England, so SE

annotation.surface: Livestock grazing on hill ridges in Kent.
annotation.walkthrough: Kent is an English county in the far south-east, which is why "Kent area" gives the compass letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the animal sense: a goat that browses is grazing on leaves and shoots.

entries.clue: Tell me to foil success (3,4,2)

blocks.note: to outwit someone is to foil them
a hit is a success

annotation.surface: A demand to reveal the plan for thwarting someone's success.
annotation.walkthrough: The join falls inside a word of the answer, so the enumeration (3,4,2) hides the two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: "Out with it!" is said to someone hesitating, demanding that they tell you.

entries.clue: Liam, Noel et al love things being what they are (5)

blocks.note: love = nil in tennis, the letter O
as is = in its present state

annotation.surface: The Gallagher brothers loving things just the way they are.
annotation.walkthrough: Liam and Noel Gallagher fronted the 1990s Manchester band, so the definition is a definition by example of its members.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Liam and Noel Gallagher were the core of the band.

entries.clue: Gunner’s noise against Othello’s back (5)

indicatorNotes.back: back means going backwards, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: v = versus, against
Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice

annotation.surface: Arsenal (the Gunners) making noise in a match against a team.
annotation.walkthrough: A gunner here is someone gunning an engine, revving it hard, not a soldier or an Arsenal fan.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: the roar of an engine being gunned is the noise its driver, the gunner, makes.

entries.clue: Watch Roman poet losing resistance (5)

indicatorNotes.losing: a poet losing something no longer has it, so that letter drops out of his name

blocks.note: Virgil, author of the Aeneid
R = resistance in physics; this R is removed

annotation.surface: An instruction to watch a Roman poet give up the fight.
annotation.walkthrough: "Watch" looks like the instruction to the solver, but it is the definition, a noun; R for resistance comes from electrical formulas.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a vigil is a watch kept, usually through the night.

entries.clue: Do the first part of it (3-2)

annotation.definition: Do the first part of it

blocks.note: not the verb but the musical note, doh
"it" is a whole note-naming system, of which do is the opening syllable

annotation.surface: An order to start a job with its first stage.
annotation.walkthrough: "Do" looks like a verb, but it is the musical note, and "it" is the tonic sol-fa system, which begins do, re, mi.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: sol-fa is the do-re-mi system of naming notes, and do comes first in it.

entries.clue: Drug designer wrongly given life (9)

indicatorNotes.wrongly: letters put together wrongly are in the wrong order, so rearrange them

blocks.note: E = ecstasy
anagram fodder with the E

annotation.surface: A designer of illicit drugs wrongly let off with a life sentence.
annotation.walkthrough: "Given life" suggests a prison term, but it means livened up. "Designer drug" also reads as one phrase, but they are separate parts.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something energised is filled with vigour, given fresh life.

entries.clue: Southern US police force remains negligent (8)

blocks.note: S = southern
the Los Angeles Police Department
ash is what remains after burning

annotation.surface: A police force in the American South that stays careless.
annotation.walkthrough: "Remains" looks like a verb (stays); it is a noun, the ash left by a fire.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: slapdash work is done hastily and carelessly, as a negligent worker does it.

entries.clue: Charlie? Waste of space, more like (6)

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a loser, a useless person

annotation.surface: An insult: Charlie is a waste of space, or near enough.
annotation.walkthrough: "Charlie" in British slang is also a fool, which makes the surface an insult; in the wordplay it is just C.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: closer means nearer the mark, more like, as in "that's more like it".
